title: Berkshire 2022 letter: business-pickers, compounding winners, and the American Tailwind
summary: Buffett explains that Berkshire's results came from about a dozen good decisions compounding over decades, not constant activity. He covers owning businesses rather than stocks, buyback math, float, honest accounting, avoiding forecasts, and Charlie Munger's wisdom.

principles.text: Buy businesses with durable economics and trustworthy managers; don't try to be a stock-picker.
principles.quote: Charlie and I are not stock-pickers; we are business-pickers.

principles.text: A few big winners dominate results over time; the weeds wither as the flowers bloom.
principles.quote: The weeds wither away in significance as the flowers bloom. Over time, it takes just a few winners to work wonders.

principles.text: Even a legendary record rests on few great decisions; most capital-allocation calls are mediocre.
principles.quote: Our satisfactory results have been the product of about a dozen truly good decisions – that would be about one every five years

principles.text: Markets are not efficient; stocks periodically trade at foolish prices, creating chances to buy wonderful businesses cheaply.
principles.quote: stocks often trade at truly foolish prices, both high and low. “Efficient” markets exist only in textbooks.

principles.text: Buybacks help continuing owners only when made below value; overpaying transfers wealth to sellers.
principles.quote: Just as surely, when a company overpays for repurchases, the continuing shareholders lose.

principles.text: Manipulating earnings to beat expectations needs only a desire to deceive, and is a shame of capitalism.
principles.quote: It requires no talent to manipulate numbers: Only a deep desire to deceive is required.
